task1.title: Household goods ownership
task1.prompt: The graph shows the percentage of households in one country that had various goods between 2001 and 2008.

chartDesc.title: Percentage of households with items
chartDesc.overview: Overall, ownership of all household goods increased between 2001 and 2008, with the sole exception of fixed telephones, which experienced a slight decrease. Mobile phones and internet access saw the most significant growth during this period.
keyFeatures: Telephones were the most common item in 2001 at 95%, but dropped slightly to 90% in 2008, tying with microwaves and CD players as the highest (90%).
Mobile phone ownership experienced the largest increase, rising from 25% in 2001 to 80% in 2008.
Internet ownership grew sixfold, from 10% in 2001 to 60% in 2008.
Dishwashers remained the least owned item in both years, rising from 20% in 2001 to 40% in 2008.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparison where relevant.
task1.sampleBand5:
The graph shows the percentage of households that had different things between 2001 and 2008. In general, most households had these things more in 2008 than in 2001.

In 2001, about 80% of households had a car. This went up to about 88% in 2008. For washing machines, it was like this too. In 2001, about 75% had a washing machine and in 2008, it was about 85%. The same thing happened with dishwashers.

However, not so many people had home computers. In 2001, it was around 35%, and in 2008 it went up to about 60%. This was a bigger increase than the others. Mobile phones also went up a lot. In 2001, around 40% of households had them, but in 2008, about 82% had a mobile phone. So, most things went up, especially mobile phones.
task1.sampleBand6:
The graph shows the percentage of houses in a country that had different appliances between 2001 and 2008. Generally, the proportion of households owning these goods increased over the period.

In 2001, the washing machine was the most common appliance, with about 80% of households owning one. This figure rose slightly to around 90% in 2008. The ownership of refrigerators also saw an increase, starting at approximately 70% and rising to about 85%. A similar pattern was observed for dishwashers, where ownership increased from roughly 40% to 60%.

However, mobile phones showed a significantly larger increase. In 2001, only 30% of households had a mobile phone. By 2008, this figure had risen dramatically to almost 80%. In contrast, the percentage of households with a vacuum cleaner remained fairly stable, fluctuating around 90% throughout the period. Overall, ownership of mobile phones saw the biggest change.
task1.sampleBand7:
The graph illustrates the proportion of households in a particular country owning several consumer goods between 2001 and 2008.

Overall, ownership of all listed items increased over the period, with mobile phones showing the most significant growth. While CD players remained relatively stable, they were overtaken by other technologies by the end of the period.

In 2001, approximately 70% of households possessed a telephone, which rose moderately to around 80% in 2008. Similarly, CD player ownership increased slightly from just under 60% to around 65%. However, mobile phone ownership witnessed a substantial surge, climbing from about 40% to nearly 80% over the seven years. Computer ownership also experienced considerable growth, rising from roughly 30% to just over 60%.

By 2008, mobile phones and telephones were the most commonly owned items, with nearly equal ownership levels. In contrast, CD players had the lowest percentage of ownership compared to the other goods. The increasing ownership of computers also demonstrates a growing trend in technology adoption during this period.
task1.sampleBand8:
The line graph illustrates the proportion of households in a particular country owning four different consumer goods over an eight-year period, from 2001 to 2008.

Overall, ownership of mobile phones and computers experienced substantial growth, while the percentage of homes with washing machines saw a marginal increase. Conversely, the prevalence of vacuum cleaners witnessed a slight decrease.

In 2001, washing machines were the most common household item, possessed by approximately 80% of households. This figure remained relatively stable throughout the period, reaching just over 80% in 2008. Mobile phone ownership, starting at around 60% in 2001, exhibited the most dramatic surge, surpassing washing machines to reach nearly 95% by 2008. Similarly, computer ownership rose significantly, from roughly 40% to about 75% over the same timeframe.

In contrast, vacuum cleaner ownership displayed a modest downward trend, declining from approximately 90% in 2001 to around 85% in 2008. Despite this decrease, vacuum cleaners remained a prevalent item in the majority of households throughout the period in question. It is also noteworthy that the rate of ownership of washing machines and vacuum cleaners was higher than that of computers and mobile phones for the first four years, before the latter two caught up and surpassed them.
task1.sampleBand9:
The graph illustrates the fluctuating ownership percentages of various household goods within a single country between 2001 and 2008. A cursory glance reveals that mobile phones experienced the most substantial growth, while washing machines exhibited the least.

In 2001, washing machine ownership was already high, at approximately 80%, experiencing only a marginal increase to around 88% by 2008. Similarly, refrigerators demonstrated a stable ownership rate, starting at roughly 60% and climbing modestly to about 75% over the period. Overall, the trend indicates a marked increase in the ownership of technology-related goods, outpacing the growth in ownership of more traditional household appliances. This suggests a shift in consumer priorities during this period.
task1.sampleAnswer:
The line graph illustrates the percentage of households owning various goods in a country over an eight-year period from 2001 to 2008. Overall, ownership of most goods increased during this time, with mobile phones showing the most dramatic growth.

In 2001, televisions were the most commonly owned item, present in approximately 98% of households, a figure that remained relatively stable throughout the period. Washing machines were found in around 75% of homes, while DVD players were in about 50% of households. Mobile phones, however, were only owned by roughly 55% of households at the start of the period.

By 2008, mobile phone ownership had surged to nearly 90%, representing the most significant increase among all the goods. DVD player ownership also grew substantially, reaching approximately 80% of households. Washing machine ownership showed modest growth, climbing to around 80%.

Interestingly, computer ownership, which started at about 45% in 2001, increased steadily to approximately 70% by 2008. The data shows a clear trend of increasing household ownership of electronic and digital goods, reflecting technological advancement and changing consumer preferences.

task2.title: Class size in language learning
task2.prompt: Some people believe that it is better language students in small classes. Others think the number of people in the classes doesn't matter. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
task2.instruction: Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
task2.sampleBand5:
Some people think small classes are better for learning languages. Other people think how many students there are doesn't matter so much. I will talk about both sides and my view.

On the one hand, small classes can be good. If there are fewer students, the teacher can give more attention to each person. They can help them with their problems and make sure they understand. Also, students might feel more comfortable to speak in a small class. They might be shy in a big class and not want to talk. This means they don't practice the language as much. So, small classes can help students learn better because they get more help and can speak more.

On the other hand, big classes can also be OK. Some people think that you can learn from other students. If there are many students, you can hear different accents and learn about different cultures. Also, big classes might be cheaper. The school doesn't need as many teachers, so they can charge less. So, even if you don't get as much attention from the teacher, you can still learn a lot in a big class. It depends on the person.

In my opinion, I think small classes are better, but only if the teacher is good. If the teacher is not very good, it doesn't matter how small the class is. But if the teacher is good and the class is small, then students can learn very well. So, I think it's important to have good teachers, but small classes can help too. It is a complex issue.
task2.sampleBand6:
There is a debate about the ideal class size for language students. Some people argue that smaller classes are more effective, while others believe that the number of students does not significantly impact learning outcomes. This essay will discuss both perspectives before giving my own opinion.

On the one hand, proponents of small classes argue that they allow for more individualized attention from the teacher. In a smaller setting, teachers can better understand each student's strengths and weaknesses, and tailor their instruction accordingly. This can lead to improved learning outcomes and increased student engagement. For example, a teacher with only ten students can easily provide personalized feedback on writing assignments, whereas a teacher with thirty students might struggle to do so. Also, shy students might feel more comfortable participating in a smaller group, which can boost their confidence and speaking skills. However, this view may be too simplistic.

On the other hand, some argue that class size is not the most important factor in language learning. They believe that the quality of the teacher, the teaching methods, and the student's own motivation are more significant. A skilled and engaging teacher can effectively manage a larger class, using techniques such as group work and peer teaching to ensure that all students are learning. Furthermore, larger classes can offer a wider range of perspectives and ideas, which can enrich the learning experience. It is also true that bigger classes can be more economical, allowing schools to invest in better resources.

In my opinion, while smaller classes can be beneficial, they are not always necessary for effective language learning. A good teacher can adapt their teaching style to suit different class sizes. The most important thing is to create a supportive and stimulating learning environment where students feel motivated to learn. To conclude, both sides have valid points, but the key to success lies in the quality of teaching and the students' willingness to learn, not just the number of students in the class.
task2.sampleBand7:
The debate surrounding the optimal class size for language learners is ongoing. While some advocate for smaller classes, believing they provide a more conducive learning environment, others argue that class size is irrelevant to the overall success of language acquisition. This essay will explore both perspectives before presenting my own view.

Proponents of small classes often highlight the benefits of increased individual attention. In a smaller setting, teachers can more easily cater to the specific needs and learning styles of each student. This personalized approach can lead to improved comprehension and retention of the material. Furthermore, smaller classes tend to foster a more relaxed and interactive atmosphere, encouraging students to participate actively and overcome their inhibitions about speaking. This is particularly beneficial for language learners who often struggle with confidence in speaking a new language. However, some might argue that this is not always the case, and a good teacher should be able to manage a larger class effectively.

Conversely, those who believe class size is inconsequential argue that other factors, such as the teacher's qualifications, the quality of the curriculum, and the student's motivation, are more significant determinants of success. They contend that a highly skilled and engaging teacher can effectively manage a larger class, providing sufficient attention and support to all students. Moreover, larger classes can offer a greater diversity of perspectives and experiences, which can enrich the learning environment and expose students to different accents and communication styles. It's also worth noting that smaller classes are not always accessible to everyone, and limiting class sizes may restrict educational opportunities.

In my opinion, while the teacher's quality and curriculum are undoubtedly crucial, class size does play a role, although not necessarily a decisive one. Ideally, a balance should be struck. While very large classes can be detrimental to individual attention, excessively small classes may lack the dynamic interaction and diverse perspectives that contribute to a stimulating learning environment. A moderate class size, coupled with a skilled teacher and a well-designed curriculum, offers the best opportunity for language learners to thrive. Ultimately, the most effective approach will vary depending on the specific context and the needs of the students.

In conclusion, both small and large classes have their merits and drawbacks. While individual attention and a relaxed atmosphere are advantages of smaller classes, the diversity and accessibility of larger classes are also important. Therefore, a nuanced approach is required, considering all relevant factors to create the most effective learning environment.
task2.sampleBand8:
The optimal learning environment for language acquisition is a subject of ongoing debate. While some advocate for small class sizes, emphasizing the benefits of personalized attention, others argue that class size is inconsequential compared to other factors. This essay will explore both perspectives before presenting my own view.

Proponents of smaller classes often highlight the enhanced opportunities for interaction between students and teachers. In a smaller setting, instructors can more readily identify individual learning styles and tailor their teaching methods accordingly. This personalized approach can be particularly beneficial for students who struggle with certain aspects of language learning, such as grammar or pronunciation. Furthermore, smaller classes foster a more intimate and supportive atmosphere, encouraging students to participate actively and overcome their inhibitions about speaking a foreign language. A concrete example would be a conversation class where each student gets ample time to practice and receive immediate feedback, something difficult to achieve in a large group.

Conversely, those who believe class size is irrelevant often point to the importance of other factors, such as teacher quality, curriculum design, and student motivation. A highly skilled and engaging teacher can effectively manage a larger class, utilizing innovative teaching techniques and technology to cater to diverse learning needs. Moreover, a well-structured curriculum that incorporates a variety of activities and resources can compensate for the lack of individual attention. Indeed, some students may even thrive in larger classes, benefiting from the diversity of perspectives and the opportunity to learn from their peers. For instance, a large class might facilitate more dynamic group discussions and collaborative projects.

In my opinion, while the aforementioned factors certainly play a crucial role, class size does have a significant impact on the learning experience, albeit not in isolation. A smaller class, while not a guaranteed recipe for success, creates a more conducive environment for personalized learning and active participation. It allows for a deeper engagement with the material and fosters a stronger sense of community among students. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that the effectiveness of any class size ultimately depends on the teacher's ability to leverage its potential and address the individual needs of their students. Therefore, a holistic approach is required, considering both class size and other pedagogical factors to optimize language learning outcomes.

task2.sampleAnswer:
The optimal size of language classes is a subject of debate among educators and students alike. While some advocate for smaller class sizes, others believe the number of students is irrelevant to learning outcomes. This essay will examine both viewpoints before offering my perspective.

Proponents of small language classes argue that they offer significant pedagogical advantages. In smaller groups, teachers can provide more individualized attention, addressing each student's specific weaknesses and learning style. Students also have more opportunities to practice speaking, which is crucial for language acquisition. Additionally, smaller classes often create a less intimidating environment where shy students feel more comfortable participating and making mistakes—an essential part of the learning process.

Conversely, those who believe class size is immaterial contend that the quality of teaching and student motivation are more important factors. A skilled teacher can effectively manage larger groups through various techniques such as pair work, group activities, and technology-assisted learning. Furthermore, learning a language is ultimately the responsibility of the individual; motivated students will succeed regardless of class size by supplementing classroom learning with self-study and practice outside of school.

In my opinion, while individual effort and teaching quality are undoubtedly important, smaller classes do provide tangible benefits for language learning. The increased speaking opportunities and personalized feedback are particularly valuable for developing fluency and accuracy. However, I acknowledge that very small classes may also lack the diversity of perspectives and interaction opportunities that slightly larger groups can provide. Therefore, I believe a moderate class size of around 10-15 students represents the ideal balance.
task2.uzSampleBand5:
Ba'zi odamlar kichik sinflar tillarni o'rganish uchun yaxshiroq deb hisoblashadi. Boshqa odamlar talabalar soni unchalik muhim emas deb o'ylashadi. Men har ikki tomon haqida ham va o'z fikrim haqida gapiraman.

Bir tomondan, kichik sinflar yaxshi bo'lishi mumkin. Agar talabalar kamroq bo'lsa, o'qituvchi har bir insonga ko'proq e'tibor bera oladi. Ular ularga muammolari bilan yordam berishlari va tushunganliklariga ishonch hosil qilishlari mumkin. Shuningdek, talabalar kichik sinfda o'zlarini qulayroq his qilishlari mumkin. Ular katta sinfda uyatchan bo'lishi va gapirishni xohlamasligi mumkin. Bu esa, ular tilni unchalik mashq qilmaydi degani. Demak, kichik sinflar talabalarga yaxshiroq o'rganishga yordam berishi mumkin, chunki ular ko'proq yordam olishadi va ko'proq gapirishlari mumkin.

Boshqa tomondan, katta sinflar ham yaxshi bo'lishi mumkin. Ba'zi odamlar siz boshqa talabalardan o'rganishingiz mumkin deb o'ylashadi. Agar ko'p talaba bo'lsa, siz turli xil lahjalarni eshitishingiz va turli madaniyatlar haqida bilib olishingiz mumkin. Shuningdek, katta sinflar arzonroq bo'lishi mumkin. Maktabga ko'p o'qituvchi kerak emas, shuning uchun ular kamroq haq olishlari mumkin. Demak, o'qituvchidan unchalik e'tibor olmasangiz ham, katta sinfda ko'p narsalarni o'rganishingiz mumkin. Bu odamga bog'liq.

Mening fikrimcha, men kichik sinflar yaxshiroq deb o'ylayman, lekin faqat agar o'qituvchi yaxshi bo'lsa. Agar o'qituvchi unchalik yaxshi bo'lmasa, sinf qanchalik kichik bo'lishining ahamiyati yo'q. Lekin agar o'qituvchi yaxshi bo'lsa va sinf kichik bo'lsa, unda talabalar juda yaxshi o'rganishlari mumkin. Demak, men yaxshi o'qituvchilarga ega bo'lish muhim deb o'ylayman, lekin kichik sinflar ham yordam berishi mumkin. Bu murakkab masala.
task2.uzSampleBand6:
Til o'rganuvchilar uchun sinfning ideal hajmi haqida bahs bor. Ba'zi odamlar kichikroq sinflar samaraliroq deb ta'kidlasa, boshqalar talabalar soni o'rganish natijalariga sezilarli ta'sir ko'rsatmaydi deb hisoblashadi. Ushbu insho ikkala nuqtai nazarni ham muhokama qiladi, so'ngra o'z fikrimni bildiraman.

Bir tomondan, kichik sinflarni yoqlab chiqadiganlar, ular o'qituvchidan individual yondashuvga imkon beradi deb ta'kidlashadi. Kichikroq muhitda o'qituvchilar har bir o'quvchining kuchli va zaif tomonlarini yaxshiroq tushunishi va shunga mos ravishda o'z ta'limotlarini moslashtirishi mumkin. Bu o'rganish natijalarining yaxshilanishiga va talabalarning ishtiyoqining oshishiga olib kelishi mumkin. Misol uchun, atigi o'nta talabasi bo'lgan o'qituvchi yozma topshiriqlar bo'yicha shaxsiy fikr-mulohazalarni osongina taqdim etishi mumkin, o'ttizta talabasi bo'lgan o'qituvchi esa buni qilishda qiynalishi mumkin.
